2026 SEMA Show • Mitsubishi Returns to Las Vegas With the Fresh 2028 Outlander Diamond Trail Edition
1-of-10 Apollo EVO, the $3.3M Caribbean Dragon, Takes Vegas by Storm With Aspirated 800-HP V12
15 photos
Photo: Apollo Automobil
How did the most artistic Greek god come to ride on the backs of dragons all the way into the New World is something only the Germans can fully understand – and explain. However, due to their not-so-vocal nature, the Germans prefer to do instead of say, so that’s how the Apollo EVO Caribbean Dragon flapped its naturally-aspirated V12 hypercar wings all the way to America.
Traditional European fire-breathing wyverns rarely appear in indigenous Caribbean folklore, where draconic legends instead manifest as primordial giant serpents and abyssal sea monsters. Among the Kalinago people of Dominica, ancient oral tales speak of Bakwa, a colossal, diamond-crested spirit serpent large enough to scale mountain cliffs and reshape volcanic terrain.
Bakwa is the trusty sidekick of Maboyo, a fearsome serpentine entity governing tropical storms, violent chaos, and the unseen destructive forces of untamed island nature. Yet the most terrifying dragon-like creature in regional lore is unquestionably the Lusca, a ruthless abyssal cryptid lurking inside the deep underwater blue holes off Andros Island in the Bahamas.
Described by mariners as a multi-headed dragon or a monstrous 200-foot shark-octopus chimera with razor-sharp teeth, the Lusca generates violent whirlpools that drag entire fishing boats and helpless swimmers down into deep submarine caverns to devour them in the dark. However, since the invention of reason has pretty much put an end to scary folklore, mythical monsters have taken a habit of going undercover.
Photo: Apollo Automobil Now, a very different breed of ferocious predator has awakened, though this mechanical mythical creature actually nests in the engineering workshops of Gaimersheim, Germany. Christened the Apollo EVO Caribbean Dragon, the carbon-fiber beast built by Germany’s only dedicated hypercar manufacturer, Apollo Automobil GmbH, has just crossed the Atlantic Ocean to North America to see what local exotic rivals and track lap records it can feast on.
Its official North American hunting ground will be the 2026 Concours at Wynn Las Vegas, where the radical new Apollo EVO is scheduled to stage its continental public debut. Running for four days from October 29 to November 1, the prestigious Nevada gathering will host this first customer production example of the track-only machine alongside two of its most celebrated predecessors from the German boutique marque’s storied high-performance stable.
The exclusive Bavarian automaker is utilizing the Las Vegas showcase to celebrate 20 years of its proud Rebellious German Engineering. For the first time outside Europe, wealthy enthusiasts and collectors will witness a complete lineage display uniting the foundational Gumpert Apollo, the visceral Apollo Intensa Emozione, and the newly completed Apollo EVO on the same lawn, illustrating the technical evolution of a track-bred automotive design philosophy.
Photo: Apollo Automobil The appearance in the United States follows the dynamic global debut of the Apollo EVO at the 2026 Goodwood Festival of Speed in England earlier this summer. Chief Executive Officer Niko Konta emphasized that North America has long remained central to the global vision of Apollo Automobil GmbH, noting that the Concours at Wynn Las Vegas offers an ideal venue to introduce the hypercar to loyal clients and passionate fans.
Conceived as a direct, track-focused successor to the acclaimed Intensa Emozione (need I translate that from Italian? It’s Intense Emotion), the Apollo EVO represents a total rejection of modern automotive homogenization. Penned by chief designer Jowyn Wong, the coupe is strictly limited to a production run of 10 customer units alongside a solitary factory prototype.
Each example is priced from €3,000,000 before local taxes and delivery fees, positioning the vehicle among the most exclusive collector machines on the planet today. That’s 3,346,000 legal money of the United States. It’s a lot of money, with which a gearhead can buy a lot of automotive adrenaline from several other high-end houses of speed, with or without electric add-ons.
Photo: Apollo Automobil Every single customer commission acts as a bespoke engineering showcase, exemplified by the inaugural Caribbean Dragon specification arriving in Las Vegas. Its sculpted exterior comprises 75 individual carbon-fiber panels finished in a white-and-blue livery through an intricate eight-layer hand-painting process that alone demands roughly 1,000 hours of labor.
That’s on top of the 1,200 hours of meticulous assembly required by specialist master technicians to construct each complete rolling chassis from the ground up. Dragons are very demanding creatures, apparently, and very much contrary to popular belief.
At the heart of the Apollo EVO sits a screaming, naturally aspirated 6.3-liter V12 engine derived from Ferrari architecture and developed in partnership with Autotecnica Motori and HWA AG. Displacing 6,262 cc and eschewing both turbochargers and hybrid electrification, the 12-cylinder powerplant revs all the way to 9,000 rpm, generating 800 hp and 765 Nm of torque (564 lb-ft) at 6,750 rpm to deliver an authentic motorsport soundtrack and immediate throttle response.
Photo: Apollo Automobil Instead of adopting a conventional dual-clutch transmission, engineers mated the high-revving engine to a racing-derived 6-speed Hewland sequential gearbox operated via an electro-pneumatic paddle-shift system. Because the entire vehicle tips the scales at just 1,300 kg, that ferocious rear-wheel-drive output propels the coupe from 0 to 62 mph in a blistering 2.7 seconds, while copious grip and stability allow the machine to reach a top speed of 208 mph (335 kph).
The visual drama on the Apollo EVO is matched by its functional aerodynamic violence, spearheaded by longitudinal aero fins and an electronically adjustable active rear spoiler. At 186 mph, the aero package generates a staggering 1,350 kg of downforce, exceeding the dry weight of the car itself.
In other words: if someone has the audacity, money, drive, and will to build a life-sized Hot Wheels track with a long-enough upside-down straight, the Apollo EVO Caribbean Dragon will casually do a flat-out inverted overhead pass. At 300 kph. I’d actually buy front-row tickets to see it happen.
Rearward airflow exits around an optional 3D-printed titanium Dragon Skin exhaust system, which naturally develops vivid blue heat patina as exhaust temperatures climb on track.
Photo: Apollo Automobil Underneath its aggressive skin, the hypercar utilizes an ultra-rigid carbon-fiber monocoque tub weighing only 105 kg, paired with carbon-ceramic disc brakes and forged center-lock wheels shod in Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 R tires.
Upward-swinging doors reveal a driver-centric, skeletonized interior architecture swathed in blue-tinted carbon fiber and white upholstery, complete with air conditioning, sensible track ergonomics, and 3 digital displays mounted directly above the bespoke racing steering wheel assembly.
This obsessive dedication to mechanical purity traces its roots back to 2004, when the company was originally established in Germany as Gumpert Sportwagenmanufaktur. The enterprise was the brainchild of Roland Gumpert, the former director of Audi Sport who had previously overseen a golden era of championship motorsport success.
Photo: Apollo Automobil Production of the brand’s inaugural model, the Gumpert Apollo, commenced in 2005, merging lightweight race engineering with strictly functional aerodynamic body design.
International stardom arrived in 2008 when a Gumpert Apollo S shattered the famous Top Gear power lap record, leaving established exotic rivals trailing in its wake. Just one year later, in 2009, the German giant-killer secured an even more prestigious accolade at the Nürburgring Nordschleife, posting a 7:11.57 lap time that beat the previous production benchmark by almost 11 seconds and stood unchallenged by competitors for nearly two full years.
Although Roland Gumpert eventually passed the torch to a new leadership team that rebranded the company as Apollo Automobil in honor of his original creation, those foundational principles remain intact. That unbroken bloodline, stretching from the 2005 Gumpert Apollo through the radical 2017 Apollo Intensa Emozione to the new 800 hp Apollo EVO Caribbean Dragon, will now take center stage for North American audiences at Wynn Las Vegas this week.
